# vstack skill catalogue

vstack 0.2.0 ships **46 skills**, **0 playbooks**, **17 principles**, **3 roles**, **7 rubrics** and **4 templates**.

Profiles: `core` 46 skills, `stack` 0, `full` 46.

## entry (3)

- **help** — Use when someone asks what the pack contains, which skill fits a task, or how to start using vstack; not for routing live work (route) or for a skill's own procedure.
- **principles** — Use when a decision needs the rule behind it, or two reasonable approaches must be adjudicated before work continues; not for a skill's procedure (help) or a project's local conventions.
- **route** — Use when a request arrives with no playbook open and the approach must be chosen before skills load; not for a one-file edit, a question a single read answers, or work whose route is already recorded.

## frame (7)

- **code-tour** — Use when someone needs to understand how existing code works — entry points, call path, state ownership — without changing it; not for explaining why a design was chosen (rationale) or for fixing it (debug).
- **figure-it-out** — Use when no playbook fits and the situation needs a bespoke sequence built from skills, with the same guarantees as a playbook; not for work that matches an existing playbook (route) or a cause that is simply unknown (debug).
- **plan** — Use when the work is framed and must be ordered into tasks with an artifact and a check each before coding starts; not for discovering what the problem is (shape) or for a situation with no known approach (figure-it-out).
- **prototype** — Use when a design question can only be answered by building something disposable and looking at it; not for answering a factual question (understand) or for production code (tdd).
- **rationale** — Use when a decision's history must be reconstructed — what was chosen, what was rejected and on what evidence; not for how the code works now (code-tour) or for making a new decision (principles).
- **shape** — Use when the request is understood but the problem is not framed — outcome, boundaries, unknowns and proof are still unstated; not for clarifying ambiguous wording (sharpen) or ordering known work (plan).
- **sharpen** — Use when a request's wording is ambiguous, its acceptance criteria are missing, or its scope is stated as a feeling; not for framing a request that is already clear (shape) or ordering agreed work (plan).

## design (9)

- **audit** — Use when an existing design, implementation or repository must be judged against stated quality attributes with evidence, rather than reviewed as a diff; not for reviewing a change (review) or for improving a measured metric (performance).
- **blueprint** — Use when an accepted design must become concrete interfaces, files and signatures that an implementer can follow without re-deciding; not for choosing the design (design) or for ordering the work (plan).
- **design** — Use when a change needs its boundaries, interfaces and data flow decided before implementation, and the decision must survive review; not for ordering known work (plan) or for auditing a design that already exists (audit).
- **forensics** — Use when a profile, trace, heap snapshot, log set or core dump must be interpreted into a cause; not for measuring an improvement (performance) or for reproducing a bug (debug).
- **impact** — Use when a proposed change needs its blast radius known — callers, contracts, data, runtime effects — before work starts; not for deciding the change (design) or for verifying it after (verify).
- **migration** — Use when stored data, a public contract or a running system must move from one shape to another without a flag day; not for a fresh implementation (design) or a same-shape refactor (refactor).
- **performance** — Use when a performance claim needs a baseline and a measured change under the same conditions; not for interpreting an existing profile (forensics) or for asserting speed without a number (evidence).
- **red-team** — Use when a design or change needs an adversary that tries to break it before users or attackers do; not for checking it meets its spec (review) or for running the gates (verify).
- **rubrics** — Use when a review needs explicit, checkable criteria instead of taste, or a pack artefact needs scoring against a fixed lens; not for performing the review itself (review) or judging whether gates pass (verify).

## build (10)

- **coverage** — Use when it is unclear whether the tests prove the acceptance criteria, or existing behaviour needs a safety net before change; not for writing the next test (tdd) or for running the gates (verify).
- **debug** — Use when a failure is reproducible but its cause is unknown, and evidence must narrow it before any fix; not for interpreting a profile (forensics) or for fixing a known cause (tdd).
- **evidence** — Use when a claim is about to be reported, committed or handed over and needs a recorded artifact behind it; not for producing the proof of a whole delivery (verify) or for writing the failing test (tdd).
- **refactor** — Use when structure must change while behaviour stays exactly the same, and the safety net must exist before the first edit; not for changing behaviour (tdd) or moving a boundary other code depends on (design).
- **tdd** — Use when behaviour must change and a test can state the expected behaviour before the implementation exists; not for characterising unknown existing behaviour (coverage) or for a disposable experiment (prototype).
- **unstick** — Use when the same failure has survived several fixes or the work keeps circling one assumption; not for a first debugging attempt (debug) or for a missing playbook (figure-it-out).
- **verify** — Use when work claims to be complete and an independent run must prove it before merge, handoff or release; not for writing the failing test first (tdd) or recording one claim (evidence).
- **verify-maintain** — Use when a project's verification commands may have drifted from the code, or a change alters how the project is checked; not for creating verification from scratch (verify-setup) or for running a delivery's gates (verify).
- **verify-setup** — Use when a project has no reliable way to prove a change works and the verification instructions must be created and made runnable; not for running existing verification (verify) or for keeping it current (verify-maintain).
- **visual-parity** — Use when a UI must match a defined reference — design file, previous build or specification — and the difference must be shown, not described; not for checking behaviour on a live page (browser-testing) or for a general review (review).

## review (5)

- **ready** — Use when work is claimed complete and someone must decide whether it is safe to merge or release, weighing gates, findings and open risks; not for producing the evidence (verify) or performing the review (review).
- **report** — Use when work must be explained to someone who did not do it — reviewer, stakeholder or future session — grounded in artifacts rather than narrative; not for compressing a session for continuation (handoff) or for publishing a release (ship).
- **review** — Use when a diff, design or document must be examined for defects before it is accepted, and findings must be specific enough to act on; not for judging a whole repository (audit) or for running the gates (verify).
- **ship** — Use when a readiness decision is made and the change must be published — merge, tag, release, deploy — with the record written as part of the act; not for deciding readiness (ready) or for watching the result afterwards (watch-pr).
- **watch-pr** — Use when a change is published and CI, review comments or a rollout must be observed until a definite outcome; not for performing the merge (ship) or for re-verifying after local changes (verify).

## continuity (6)

- **decisions** — Use when a choice will matter later and must be recorded with its alternatives, evidence and consequences so it is not relitigated; not for reconstructing an old decision (rationale) or for applying a rule (principles).
- **handoff** — Use when work pauses and the next session or person must continue without re-reading the history, or when work must stop in a state that is safe and honestly described; not for explaining results to a stakeholder (report) or for restoring a broken state (recovery).
- **lessons** — Use when the same mistake has happened twice, or an incident or delivery revealed a rule that should change the method itself; not for recording what happened (report) or for a one-off fix (debug).
- **recovery** — Use when work was interrupted mid-operation or a change must be undone, and the system must return to a known-good state before anything else; not for pausing safely (handoff) or for re-verifying finished work (verify).
- **resume** — Use when picking up work from a previous session, another agent or a recorded handoff, and the current state must be validated before continuing; not for starting new work (route) or for restoring a broken state (recovery).
- **worktree** — Use when work needs isolation from the main checkout — a parallel task, a risky change, a review of someone else's branch — and the workspace must be created, inspected or removed safely; not for handing over work in progress (handoff) or recovering a broken checkout (recovery).

## meta (3)

- **skill-authoring** — Use when a new skill must be written or an existing one reshaped to the pack's standard, with a trigger description, a procedure and an evaluation; not for scoring whether a skill fires (skill-eval) or for editing playbooks (maintain-playbook).
- **skill-eval** — Use when it is unclear whether a skill fires on the right requests or its procedure produces the claimed output; not for writing the skill (skill-authoring) or for scoring a delivery (rubrics).
- **unslop** — Use when generated or accumulated code has become more complex than the problem — duplication, dead paths, speculative abstraction — and must be reduced without changing behaviour; not for improving structure with tests as the goal (refactor) or for reviewing correctness (review).
